prompt.context: The year is 1999, in the middle of the dot-com boom. An airline has been approached by a group of entrepreneurs. The entrepreneurs are offering the airline two things simultaneously: (1) invest $100MM in their software company for a 20% equity stake, and (2) become the first customer for the software they are developing. The software is an e-marketplace where airlines and spare-parts suppliers can meet to improve purchasing capabilities and reduce purchasing costs. Aircraft parts are a hugely important part of the airline business, as airlines struggle to keep planes in the air as much as possible, minimize downtime, and control costs.
prompt.question: What should the airline do?

clarifying_info.q: How does the airline currently purchase spare parts?
clarifying_info.a: The airline currently has a legacy system that is not well-suited to what is actually happening, so there is a lot of extra phone calls and process work involved.

clarifying_info.q: How much does a purchasing transaction currently cost the airline?
How many transactions does each airline perform every year?
clarifying_info.a: 500,000 transactions per year for each airline in the US.

clarifying_info.q: How many airlines are there in the US?
How much will a transaction cost in the new system?
clarifying_info.a: $6 payment to the software company per transaction, plus $9 in internal costs (labor, systems, etc.) — total $15 per transaction.

clarifying_info.q: Is there any other cost to join the system?
What is the cost structure for the software company?
clarifying_info.a: No variable costs. $10MM per year in fixed corporate expenses.

clarifying_info.q: Will the e-marketplace give the airline increased bargaining power over suppliers?
clarifying_info.a: No. The aircraft spare-parts industry is highly regulated. Becoming an approved FAA supplier is expensive, so barriers to entry are significant. Each part typically has only one or two suppliers, so bargaining power will not improve through the e-marketplace.

exhibits.title: E-Market Structure
exhibits.shows: A diagram of the e-marketplace, showing a central E-Market hub connected to Supplier 1 through Supplier 1000 on one side and Airline 1 through Airline 20 on the other side.

framework: Decouple the two distinct decisions: (A) investment decision — should the airline invest $100MM for 20% equity? and (B) customer decision — should the airline use the software as a customer (first or later)?
Investment analysis: model cash flows for the 20% equity stake — revenues, costs, net income, our share, payback period, and NPV vs. the $100MM outlay.
Customer analysis: model cost savings from switching to the new system — current cost per transaction vs. new cost, annual savings, payback on the $20MM licensing fee.
Market and competitive context: network effects (supplier coverage), competitive dynamics, regulatory environment, and risk of being first customer.
Synthesize: make a clear recommendation on each of the two decisions separately, with supporting numbers and key risks.

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual cash flow attributable to the airline's 20% equity stake in the software company.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates set up a DCF/cash-flow timeline from year 0 onward. They derive: revenue = $6 x 500,000 x 20 = $60MM; less fixed costs of $10MM = $50MM net; 20% share = $10MM/year. They then assess value: payback without discounting is 10 years ($100MM / $10MM). Using a high software-industry discount rate (~20%), NPV = $10MM / 0.20 = $50MM, versus the $100MM invested — a bad investment. Candidates should flag that using the airline's low discount rate would be wrong; the appropriate rate reflects the risk of a dot-com software startup.

math.setup: Annual revenue to software company = transaction fee x transactions per airline x number of airlines. Net income = revenue - fixed costs. Airline's share = net income x equity stake. Investment NPV = share / discount rate.
steps: Invested $100MM for something worth $50MM at the moment of investment → value destruction
math.answer: $10MM annual cash flow; NPV of ~$50MM vs. $100MM invested — a poor investment.

questions.prompt: Calculate the annual cost savings for the airline as a customer of the e-marketplace, and assess the payback on the $20MM licensing fee.
questions.guidance: Candidates should compute: current cost $50/transaction, new cost $6 + $9 = $15/transaction, savings $35/transaction. Annual savings = $35 x 500,000 = $17.5MM. Payback on $20MM licensing fee = $20MM / $17.5MM ≈ 1.1 years — an excellent return. However, strong candidates also note the risks of being the FIRST customer: suppliers may not join immediately; software may have bugs early on; the startup could go bankrupt, forfeiting the licensing fee with no return.

math.setup: Cost savings per transaction = current cost - new cost. Annual savings = savings per transaction x annual transactions. Payback = licensing fee / annual savings.
steps: New cost per transaction = $6 (platform fee) + $9 (internal costs) = $15
math.answer: $17.5MM annual savings; payback in ~1.1 years — financially attractive as a customer.

questions.prompt: (Challenge question) The software has a feature allowing airlines to view other airlines' spare-parts inventory by location. Is this a good feature?
questions.guidance: A full answer covers: (1) benefit — the whole industry reduces downtime by sharing inventory, e.g. Southwest can buy a part in NYC from American Airlines instead of waiting 3 days for a supplier shipment; (2) risk — the feature may encourage airlines to carry zero inventory ('why hold parts when everyone shares?'); (3) mitigation — a system of checks and balances via a parts-exchange account for each airline: each time an airline takes a part, its account is debited by the part cost; each time it provides a part, it is credited. Capping the minimum balance (e.g. at -$5MM) prevents free-riding and encourages responsible inventory management.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the key risks of being the first customer for this e-marketplace?

categories.name: Supplier network risk
ideas: Not all suppliers will join immediately or at all, limiting the platform's utility
Network effects mean value is low until critical mass of suppliers is reached
Highly regulated FAA-approved suppliers may be slow to onboard

categories.name: Technology / execution risk
ideas: Software will likely have bugs in the first months or years
Integration with the airline's legacy systems may be costly and time-consuming
The startup may lack the engineering capacity to support 20 airlines simultaneously at launch

categories.name: Financial / counterparty risk
ideas: The software company could go bankrupt, forfeiting the $20MM licensing fee
Dot-com valuations are inflated; the startup's long-term viability is uncertain
The equity investment ($100MM) has poor NPV — being a customer is separate but the two deals are bundled

categories.name: Competitive / strategic risk
ideas: Competitors who join later avoid early-adopter costs and bugs but still capture benefits
No improvement in bargaining power due to limited FAA-approved supplier pool
Being locked into one platform creates switching costs if a better solution emerges

recommendation: Do NOT make the $100MM equity investment: the undiscounted payback is 10 years and the NPV (~$50MM) is half the investment amount, making it a value-destroying deal for the airline.
Becoming a customer (paying the $20MM licensing fee) is financially compelling — payback in ~1.1 years — but the airline should NOT be the first customer given the early-adopter risks.
Instead, let other airlines join first; once the software is proven and supplier coverage is sufficient, the airline should join as a customer to capture the $17.5MM/year in cost savings.
risks: First-customer risks: bugs, limited supplier coverage, startup bankruptcy
No bargaining power improvement due to FAA-regulated supplier concentration
Dot-com environment inflates startup valuations; 20% for $100MM may be overpriced
Joining later means forgoing savings in the interim, but avoids downside risks
next_steps: Negotiate to separate the investment deal from the customer deal — they need not be bundled
If the airline does join as a first customer, negotiate risk-sharing (e.g. reduced licensing fee, money-back guarantee, equity in lieu of cash)
Monitor competitor adoption; join as a customer once 2-3 airlines have validated the platform
